\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Low-degree Fourier family]
\lean{FABL.lowDegreeFourierFamily}
\statementsource{lmn-constant-depth-fourier}{pdf-63759bd909d5-p004-b006}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p069-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p089-b006,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p215-b009,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p215-b010
}
\label{FABL.lowDegreeFourierFamily}
\leanok
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the low-degree Fourier family consists of all subsets
of the $n$ coordinates whose cardinality is at most $k$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Membership in the low-degree Fourier family]
\lean{FABL.mem_lowDegreeFourierFamily}
\label{FABL.mem_lowDegreeFourierFamily}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.lowDegreeFourierFamily}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ and $k$ be natural numbers, and let $S$ be a subset of the $n$ coordinates. Then
$S$ belongs to the family of sets of size at most $k$ if and only if $|S|\\le k$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Nonemptiness of the low degree family]
\lean{FABL.lowDegreeFourierFamily_nonempty}
\label{FABL.lowDegreeFourierFamily_nonempty}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.lowDegreeFourierFamily}
\difficulty{1}
For all nonnegative integers $n$ and $k$, the family of subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ of
size at most $k$ is nonempty.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Counting subsets of bounded size]
\lean{FABL.card_lowDegreeFourierFamily_eq_sum_choose}
\label{FABL.card_lowDegreeFourierFamily_eq_sum_choose}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.lowDegreeFourierFamily}
\difficulty{4}
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the number of subsets of an $n$-element set having size
at most $k$ is $\sum_{j=0}^{k}\binom{n}{j}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Bound for the number of low degree subsets]
\lean{FABL.card_lowDegreeFourierFamily_le}
\label{FABL.card_lowDegreeFourierFamily_le}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.card_lowDegreeFourierFamily_eq_sum_choose, FABL.lowDegreeFourierFamily}
\difficulty{4}
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the number of subsets of an $n$-element set having size
at most $k$ is at most $(k+1)(n+1)^k$.
\end{theorem}

  {FABL.mem_lowDegreeFourierFamily}

  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p081-b003,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p081-b004}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ and $k$ be natural numbers, and let $f$ be a real-valued function on the
$n$-dimensional sign cube. The sum of its squared Fourier coefficients over sets outside
the family of all coordinate sets of size at most $k$ equals the sum over coordinate
sets of size greater than $k$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{1}
Let $n,k\ge 0$, let $f:\{\pm1\}^n\to\mathbb R$, and let $\varepsilon\in\mathbb R$. The
total squared Fourier weight on sets of cardinality greater than $k$ is at most
$\varepsilon$ if and only if the Fourier weight outside the family of all sets of
cardinality at most $k$ is at most $\varepsilon$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Monotonicity of Fourier weight tails]
\lean{FABL.fourierWeightAboveReal_antitone}
\label{FABL.fourierWeightAboveReal_antitone}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.fourierCoeff, FABL.fourierWeightAboveReal}
\difficulty{3}
Let $f$ be any real-valued function on the $n$-dimensional sign cube, and let
$a,b\in\mathbb{R}$ with $a\le b$. The sum of squared Fourier coefficients of $f$ over
subsets whose cardinality is greater than $b$ is at most the corresponding sum over
subsets whose cardinality is greater than $a$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Monotonicity in the degree cutoff]
\lean{FABL.IsFourierSpectrumConcentratedUpTo.mono_cutoff}
\label{FABL.IsFourierSpectrumConcentratedUpTo.mono_cutoff}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.IsFourierSpectrumConcentratedUpTo, FABL.fourierWeightAboveReal_antitone}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $f:\\{−1,1\\}^n\\to\\mathbb R$, and let
$\\varepsilon,a,b\\in\\mathbb R$ with $a\\le b$. If the sum of squared Fourier
coefficients over coordinate sets whose size is strictly greater than $a$ is at most
$\\varepsilon$, then the corresponding sum over sets whose size is strictly greater than
$b$ is also at most $\\varepsilon$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Monotonicity in the error bound]
\lean{FABL.IsFourierSpectrumConcentratedUpTo.mono_error}
\label{FABL.IsFourierSpectrumConcentratedUpTo.mono_error}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.IsFourierSpectrumConcentratedUpTo}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $f:\\{−1,1\\}^n\\to\\mathbb R$, and let
$\\varepsilon,\\varepsilon',k\\in\\mathbb R$ with $\\varepsilon\\le\\varepsilon'$. If
the sum of squared Fourier coefficients over coordinate sets whose size is strictly
greater than $k$ is at most $\\varepsilon$, then that sum is at most $\\varepsilon'$ as
well.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Degree from total influence]
\lean{FABL.totalInfluenceLearningDegree}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p069-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p095-b005
}
\label{FABL.totalInfluenceLearningDegree}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.PositiveLearningParameter}
For a real number $t$ and a rational parameter $\varepsilon$ with $0<\varepsilon\leq
1/2$, define the learning degree to be the least natural number greater than or equal to
$2t/\varepsilon$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Degree from noise sensitivity]
\lean{FABL.noiseSensitivityLearningDegree}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p070-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p130-b006,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p131-b001
}
\label{FABL.noiseSensitivityLearningDegree}
\leanok
For a real number $\delta$, define the learning degree to be the least natural number
greater than or equal to $1/\delta$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Noise sensitivity bounds Fourier tail]
\lean{FABL.isFourierSpectrumConcentratedUpTo_noiseSensitivityLearningDegree}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p070-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p070-b004
}
\label{FABL.isFourierSpectrumConcentratedUpTo_noiseSensitivityLearningDegree}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.IsFourierSpectrumConcentratedUpTo, FABL.IsFourierSpectrumConcentratedUpTo.mono_cutoff, FABL.IsFourierSpectrumConcentratedUpTo.mono_error, FABL.PositiveLearningParameter, FABL.isFourierSpectrumConcentratedUpTo_noiseSensitivity, FABL.noiseSensitivity, FABL.noiseSensitivityLearningDegree, FABL.two_div_one_sub_exp_neg_two_mul_noiseSensitivity_le_three}
\difficulty{4}
Let $f$ be a Boolean function on the sign cube $␀{-1,1}^{n}$, let $␀delta$ be a real
number with $0<␀delta␀le 1/2$, and let $␀varepsilon␀in␀mathbb{Q}$ satisfy
$0<␀varepsilon<1/2$. If the probability that $f$ changes when each coordinate is
independently flipped with probability $␀delta$ is at most $␀varepsilon/6$, then the sum
of squared Fourier coefficients indexed by subsets $S$ with $|S|>␀lceil 1/␀delta␀rceil$
is at most $␀varepsilon/2$.
\end{theorem}

For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, and a rational parameter $\varepsilon$ with

\begin{definition}[Monotone learning degree]
\lean{FABL.monotoneLearningDegree}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p081-b007}

\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.PositiveLearningParameter, FABL.majority, FABL.totalInfluence, FABL.totalInfluenceLearningDegree}
For a natural number $n$ and a rational parameter $\varepsilon$ with $0<\varepsilon\leq
1/2$, define the monotone learning degree by applying the degree-from-total-influence
rule to the total influence of majority on $n$ coordinates and parameter $\varepsilon$.
\end{definition}

\lean{FABL.decisionTreeLearningDegree}

of coordinates, and let $\varepsilon$ be rational with $0<\varepsilon\leq 1/2$. Define

leaves of $T$ and the threshold $\varepsilon/2$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Degree-dependent Fourier granularity]
\lean{FABL.degreeFourierGranularity}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p036-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p089-b003
}
\label{FABL.degreeFourierGranularity}
\leanok
For each natural number $k$, define the granularity to be $2(1/2)^k$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Positivity of Fourier granularity]
\lean{FABL.degreeFourierGranularity_pos}
\label{FABL.degreeFourierGranularity_pos}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.degreeFourierGranularity}
\difficulty{3}
For every natural number $k$, the Fourier granularity at level $k$ is positive.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Real-valued granularity formula]
\lean{FABL.degreeFourierGranularity_cast}
\label{FABL.degreeFourierGranularity_cast}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.degreeFourierGranularity}
\difficulty{2}
For every natural number $k$, the real value of the degree-$k$ Fourier granularity is
$2(1/2)^k$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Rounding to Fourier granularity]
\lean{FABL.roundToDegreeFourierGranularity}
\label{FABL.roundToDegreeFourierGranularity}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.degreeFourierGranularity}
For a natural number $k$ and a rational number $q$, round $q$ divided by the degree-$k$
Fourier granularity to the nearest integer, then multiply by that granularity. (The
defining construction of the degree-$k$ Fourier granularity is not included in the
supplied statement.)
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Rounding to Fourier granularity]
\lean{FABL.roundToDegreeFourierGranularity_eq_of_close}
\label{FABL.roundToDegreeFourierGranularity_eq_of_close}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.degreeFourierGranularity, FABL.degreeFourierGranularity_pos, FABL.roundToDegreeFourierGranularity}
\difficulty{4}
For an integer $k\ge 0$, let $g_k=2(1/2)^k$. If $q\in\mathbb Q$ and $z\in\mathbb Z$
satisfy $|q-zg_k|<g_k/2$, then rounding $q$ to the nearest multiple of $g_k$ gives
$zg_k$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Degree-dependent coefficient accuracy]
\lean{FABL.degreeFourierCoefficientAccuracy}
\statementsource{lmn-constant-depth-fourier}{
  pdf-63759bd909d5-p010-b002,
  pdf-63759bd909d5-p010-b005
}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p036-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p090-b002
}
\label{FABL.degreeFourierCoefficientAccuracy}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.PositiveLearningParameter, FABL.degreeFourierGranularity, FABL.degreeFourierGranularity_pos}
For each natural number $k$, define the coefficient accuracy to be one quarter of the
degree-$k$ Fourier granularity; this is a rational number strictly between $0$ and
$1/2$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Exact coefficient accuracy]
\lean{FABL.degreeFourierCoefficientAccuracy_value}
\label{FABL.degreeFourierCoefficientAccuracy_value}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.degreeFourierCoefficientAccuracy, FABL.degreeFourierGranularity}
\difficulty{3}
For every natural number $k$, the coefficient accuracy parameter is $2^{-(k+1)}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Sample count per Fourier coefficient]
\lean{FABL.exactDegreeSamplesPerCoefficient}
\label{FABL.exactDegreeSamplesPerCoefficient}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.degreeFourierCoefficientAccuracy, FABL.finiteFamilyCoefficientConfidence, FABL.fourierEstimatorSampleCount, FABL.lowDegreeFourierFamily, FABL.lowDegreeFourierFamily_nonempty}
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the exact-degree sample count per coefficient is the
Fourier estimator sample count at the degree-$k$ coefficient accuracy, using the
finite-family coefficient confidence for the low-degree Fourier family on $n$
coordinates and its stated nonemptiness witness.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Exact-degree Fourier estimator output]
\lean{FABL.exactDegreeFourierEstimatorOutput}
\statementsource{lmn-constant-depth-fourier}{pdf-63759bd909d5-p010-b002}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p080-b002}
\label{FABL.exactDegreeFourierEstimatorOutput}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.SparseFourierHypothesis, FABL.SparseFourierHypothesis.ofCoefficients, FABL.empiricalFourierCoeff, FABL.exactDegreeSamplesPerCoefficient, FABL.lowDegreeFourierFamily, FABL.roundToDegreeFourierGranularity}
Let $n$ and $k$ be natural numbers, and let $f$ assign a sign in $\{-1,1\\}$ to each
point of the $n$-dimensional Boolean cube. For each set of coordinates of size at most
$k$, provide the prescribed number of cube inputs, and form their labels by evaluating
$f$ on those inputs. The estimator returns a sparse Fourier hypothesis supported on the
sets of coordinates of size at most $k$, with each coefficient obtained by rounding the
empirical Fourier coefficient from its supplied inputs to the degree-$k$ Fourier
granularity.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Exact Fourier coefficients of the estimator]
\lean{FABL.exactDegreeFourierEstimatorOutput_coefficient_cast_eq}
\label{FABL.exactDegreeFourierEstimatorOutput_coefficient_cast_eq}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.degreeFourierCoefficientAccuracy, FABL.degreeFourierGranularity, FABL.degreeFourierGranularity_cast, FABL.degreeFourierGranularity_pos, FABL.empiricalFourierCoeff, FABL.empiricalFourierCoeff_cast, FABL.exactDegreeFourierEstimatorOutput, FABL.exactDegreeSamplesPerCoefficient, FABL.finiteFamilyCoefficientBadSetWithParameters, FABL.finiteFamilyCoefficientConfidence, FABL.fourierCoeff, FABL.fourierDegree, FABL.isFourierGranular_signValue_of_fourierDegree_le, FABL.lowDegreeFourierFamily, FABL.lowDegreeFourierFamily_nonempty, FABL.realEmpiricalFourierCoeff, FABL.roundToDegreeFourierGranularity, FABL.roundToDegreeFourierGranularity_eq_of_close, FABL.signValue}
\difficulty{5}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $f:\{\pm1\}^n\to\{\pm1\}$, and let $k\ge1$ satisfy that
every set in the Fourier support of the real-valued sign representation of $f$ has size
at most $k$. For each subset $S\subseteq[n]$ with $|S|\le k$, choose a batch of the
prescribed number of inputs, and suppose that for every such $S$ the empirical Fourier
coefficient differs from the true Fourier coefficient of $f$ by strictly less than the
estimator's accuracy parameter. Then, for every such $S$, the estimator's rational
coefficient for $S$, viewed as a real number, equals the true Fourier coefficient of
$f$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Exact real-valued recovery]
\lean{FABL.exactDegreeFourierEstimatorOutput_realValue_eq}
\label{FABL.exactDegreeFourierEstimatorOutput_realValue_eq}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.SparseFourierHypothesis.realValue, FABL.degreeFourierCoefficientAccuracy, FABL.exactDegreeFourierEstimatorOutput, FABL.exactDegreeFourierEstimatorOutput_coefficient_cast_eq, FABL.exactDegreeSamplesPerCoefficient, FABL.finiteFamilyCoefficientBadSetWithParameters, FABL.finiteFamilyCoefficientConfidence, FABL.fourierCoeff, FABL.fourierDegree, FABL.fourierDegree_le_iff, FABL.fourier_expansion, FABL.lowDegreeFourierFamily, FABL.lowDegreeFourierFamily_nonempty, FABL.monomial}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $f:\{\pm1\}^n\to\{\pm1\}$, and let $k\ge1$ satisfy that
every set in the Fourier support of the real-valued sign representation of $f$ has size
at most $k$. For each subset $S\subseteq[n]$ with $|S|\le k$, choose a batch of the
prescribed number of inputs, and suppose that for every such $S$ the empirical Fourier
coefficient differs from the true Fourier coefficient of $f$ by strictly less than the
estimator's accuracy parameter. The real-valued function represented by the estimator's
sparse Fourier hypothesis then equals the real-valued sign representation of $f$ at
every input.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Exact recovery by the Fourier estimator]
\lean{FABL.exactDegreeFourierEstimatorOutput_evaluate_eq}
\label{FABL.exactDegreeFourierEstimatorOutput_evaluate_eq}
\leanok

\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $f:\{\pm1\}^n\to\{\pm1\}$, and let $k\ge1$ satisfy that
every set in the Fourier support of the real-valued sign representation of $f$ has size
at most $k$. For each subset $S\subseteq[n]$ with $|S|\le k$, choose a batch of the
prescribed number of inputs, and suppose that for every such $S$ the empirical Fourier
coefficient differs from the true Fourier coefficient of $f$ by strictly less than the
estimator's accuracy parameter. The Boolean function obtained by thresholding the

\begin{definition}[Labeled exact-degree estimator output]
\lean{FABL.exactDegreeFourierEstimatorLabeledOutput}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p080-b002}
\label{FABL.exactDegreeFourierEstimatorLabeledOutput}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.SparseFourierHypothesis, FABL.SparseFourierHypothesis.ofCoefficients, FABL.empiricalFourierCoeff, FABL.exactDegreeSamplesPerCoefficient, FABL.lowDegreeFourierFamily, FABL.roundToDegreeFourierGranularity}
Let $n$ and $k$ be natural numbers. For each set of coordinates of size at most $k$,
supply the prescribed number of labeled examples, each consisting of a point of the
$n$-dimensional Boolean cube and a sign. The output is a sparse Fourier hypothesis
supported on those coordinate sets, with each coefficient obtained by rounding the
empirical Fourier coefficient computed from the supplied examples to the degree-$k$
Fourier granularity.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Exact-degree Fourier estimator program]
\lean{FABL.exactDegreeFourierEstimatorProgram}
\statementsource{lmn-constant-depth-fourier}{
  pdf-63759bd909d5-p010-b001,
  pdf-63759bd909d5-p010-b002
}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p080-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p080-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p090-b002
}
\label{FABL.exactDegreeFourierEstimatorProgram}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.LearningProgram, FABL.SparseFourierHypothesis, FABL.exactDegreeFourierEstimatorLabeledOutput, FABL.exactDegreeSamplesPerCoefficient, FABL.lowDegreeFourierFamily}
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, define a random-example learning program that draws a
matrix of labeled examples, with one row for each set of coordinates of size at most $k$
and the prescribed number of samples in each row. It returns the exact-degree Fourier
estimator output from this matrix and charges local work equal to the number of such
coordinate sets times the sample count per coefficient times $n+1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Law of the degree-bounded Fourier estimator]
\lean{FABL.runWithCost_exactDegreeFourierEstimatorProgram}
\label{FABL.runWithCost_exactDegreeFourierEstimatorProgram}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.LearningProgram.randomExampleMatrixOutputLaw, FABL.LearningProgram.runWithCost, FABL.exactDegreeFourierEstimatorLabeledOutput, FABL.exactDegreeFourierEstimatorProgram, FABL.exactDegreeSamplesPerCoefficient, FABL.lowDegreeFourierFamily}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n,k\in\mathbb N$, and let $f:\{\pm1\}^n\to\{\pm1\}$ be a target function. The law
of the degree-$k$ Fourier estimator program is the law obtained by drawing,
independently and uniformly, one batch of labeled examples for each subset
$S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ with $|S|\le k$, then returning the hypothesis whose
coefficient at $S$ is the empirical Fourier coefficient rounded to granularity
$2^{1-k}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Cost of the Fourier estimation program]
\lean{FABL.exactDegreeFourierEstimatorProgram_cost_eq}
\label{FABL.exactDegreeFourierEstimatorProgram_cost_eq}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.LearningCost, FABL.LearningProgram.randomExampleMatrixOutputLaw, FABL.LearningProgram.runWithCost, FABL.SparseFourierHypothesis, FABL.exactDegreeFourierEstimatorProgram, FABL.exactDegreeSamplesPerCoefficient, FABL.lowDegreeFourierFamily, FABL.runWithCost_exactDegreeFourierEstimatorProgram}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n,k$ be natural numbers, let $f:\{\pm1\}^n\to\{\pm1\}$, and let $(H,C)$ be an
outcome in the support of the probability distribution produced by the exact-degree
Fourier estimation program on target $f$. Then its cost is $C=\bigl(|\mathcal
F|m,\,0,\,|\mathcal F|m+|\mathcal F|m(n+1)\bigr)$, where $\mathcal F$ is the family of
subsets of $[n]$ of size at most $k$ and $m$ is the program's prescribed number of
samples per subset.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Upper bound on the sample count]
\lean{FABL.exactDegreeSamplesPerCoefficient_cast_le}
\label{FABL.exactDegreeSamplesPerCoefficient_cast_le}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.degreeFourierCoefficientAccuracy, FABL.exactDegreeSamplesPerCoefficient, FABL.finiteFamilyCoefficientConfidence, FABL.fourierEstimatorFailureBits, FABL.fourierEstimatorSampleCount_cast_le, FABL.lowDegreeFourierFamily, FABL.lowDegreeFourierFamily_nonempty}
\difficulty{1}
For all natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the number of samples prescribed per coefficient by
the exact-degree estimator, viewed as a rational number, is at most $4B/\varepsilon^2$,
where $B$ is the failure-bit count at the confidence parameter assigned to the family of
subsets of $[n]$ of size at most $k$, and $\varepsilon$ is the estimator's degree-$k$
accuracy parameter.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Fourier degree bounded by decision tree depth]
\lean{FABL.fourierDegree_toReal_le_depth_of_decisionTree}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p074-b005}
\label{FABL.fourierDegree_toReal_le_depth_of_decisionTree}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.F₂DecisionTree, FABL.F₂DecisionTree.Computes, FABL.F₂DecisionTree.depth, FABL.F₂DecisionTree.vectorFourierDegree_le_depth_of_computes, FABL.binaryCubeSignEquiv, FABL.binaryFunctionOnSignCube, FABL.fourierDegree, FABL.vectorFourierDegree}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $h:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{ -1,1\}$, and let $T$ be a finite
binary decision tree whose internal nodes query coordinates from a subset of the $n$
input coordinates and whose leaves return real numbers. Suppose that, on every binary
input $x\in\{0,1\}^n$, the tree returns the real value of $h$ at the corresponding sign
input, obtained by replacing each bit $0$ by $1$ and each bit $1$ by $-1$. Then the
Fourier degree of the real-valued sign function $h$ is at most the depth of $T$.
\end{theorem}
